title: Benny Carter at Small's Paradise, then the cutting contest with Hodges
summary: Hodges sent them to hear Benny Carter at Small's, which left him cold, but at a 129th Street cutting contest Carter played superbly against Hodges.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: Tell me. When you came down to the Savoy, Johnny Hodges told you to go over to Small's Paradise and listen to Benny Carter...

No. He said, 'Go over to Small's Paradise and listen to the greatest saxophone player in the world. His name is Benny.' So Harry and I, we went there. And we walked up to the bandstand... The bandstand was low, right

down on the floor. We walked up to the bandstand. By Benny Waters being in the band, we knew Benny, and we walked up and said, "Hey, Benny." And all three of them, the reed section, stood up and says, "Hi. Hi." I looked at Benny Waters... I don't know these other two Bennies, you know.
So they laughed. And Benny Waters introduced us to Ben Witt and Benny Carter. So it was funny. All three of them stood up when we said, "Hey, Benny!" But Benny didn't move me that night.
No. You know, Benny was...he played what he wanted to play.
But he moved you later on. You heard him later.

Oh yeah! Ha. Because, that night he was... You know, he'd be playing and he'd have an eyeshade on his eyes, like an old-time gambling house men used to deal the cards -- they'd have a thing around their head to shade the light on them. So he used to have that on his eyes. And he'd be sleeping most of the time. Benny would be sitting up there on the edge of the bandstand, and he'd be sound asleep. So this must have been one of them nights he didn't feel good, because he wasn't playin' nothin'. And when he played something, it didn't sound like anything to me. I had come to hear him, you know, because he could play
something -- you know, the world's greatest. He didn't move me a bit. I told Harry, "I don't know, I don't think too much of him." I didn't know him. But I didn't think too much of him.

Well, later, they were having a cutting contest at a bar at 129th Street, and I walked in. And there wasn't but two saxophones there, with their horns out, and that was Johnny Hodges and Benny Carter. And Johnny was playing when I came in... Boy, he was beautiful. Oh, he was playin'! Then Benny started to play. Well, see, Benny's style was altogether different. There was no similarity about their styles at all. Nothing was the same. And Benny got to playing, them funny jumps and things that he makes -- the most beautiful thing you ever want to hear in your life. And I said, "This guy can play. Man, Johnny wasn't lying when he said he's the greatest in the world." I said, "I won't say he's the greatest, but he ain't far from being second!" Boy, he played, and Johnny would play again... Oh, they were awesome(?).

Oh, Benny could play. Benny knows what he's playing. See, Johnny a lot of times, he couldn't explain to you what he's doing. But with Benny, he knows everything he's doing. So that was really a night. And the funny thing, no other saxophones were playing.
No. Me? What? Are you kidding? We had some good times around New York.
